title: Nepal: FAN concludes 34th Annual General Meeting, 4th International Flora Expo to be held in March - FloralDaily
description: Nepal: FAN concludes 34th Annual General Meeting, 4th International Flora Expo to be held in March  FloralDaily
publisher.title: FloralDaily
full_article:
The 34th Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Floriculture Association Nepal (FAN) has been successfully concluded. The program was held under the chairmanship of FAN President Rajesh Bhakta Shrestha, with Anjan Shrestha, President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), as the chief guest.

The event was attended by FNCCI Vice President and Chairperson of the Commodity Council Naresh Lal Shrestha; Senior Horticulture Development Officer at the National Fruit Development Centre Srijana Paudel; Chairperson of the Agriculture Enterprise Centre Shiva Prasad Ghimire; former FAN President Min Bahadur Tamang; President of the Nepal Agricultural Machinery Business Association Krishna Sharma; representatives of various organizations; flower entrepreneurs; and office bearers of the association.

Highlighting the need for mutual support during the current period of natural disasters, FNCCI President Anjan Shrestha stated that all stakeholders should extend a helping hand to one another to increase the production and productivity of Nepali products. He also stated that FNCCI has always been at the forefront of supporting the development of Nepal's floriculture sector.

Speaking at the 34th AGM, FAN President Rajesh Bhakta Shrestha announced that the association is preparing to organize the 4th International Flora Expo-in March25 to 28, 2027. He stated that the exhibition is being organized with the objective of promoting, protecting, and commercializing Nepal's floriculture sector, as well as expanding the reach of flowers and flower-related products in national and international markets.

title: Tibet-Nepal Mudslide: The shocking cost of climate destruction, imperialism and dictatorship - 社會主義行動
description: Tibet-Nepal Mudslide: The shocking cost of climate destruction, imperialism and dictatorship  社會主義行動
publisher.title: 社會主義行動
full_article:
More than one thousand dead in Nepal – no credible death toll yet reported on the Chinese side

chinaworker.info reporters

The horror of the Himalayan disaster of August 26-27, on the border between Tibet and Nepal, was expressed by one woman who narrowly escaped when the bus she was travelling in was swept away: “It was water mixed with mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us.”

This was one of the most severe natural disasters to strike the Himalayan region in recent years. A massive glacial collapse occurred on the northern slope of Langtang Lirung peak in Nepal, at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres. Ice and underlying bedrock crashed down at high speed, carrying with it mud and debris from the mountainside, creating a colossal mudslide and flash floods that raced down the river valley on the Tibetan side of the border, then striking the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and the Rasuwa district of Nepal. It crashed through the Trishula River valley for 72 kilometres, bringing death and unfathomable destruction. Some of the dead bodies were carried into India, 150 kilometres downstream.

Initially, seismologists mistook the incident for a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. The force of the collapsing rock and ice triggered a 5.2 reading on the Richter scale – equal in power to the Hiroshima atom bomb. Wherever the mudslide passed, villages, roads, bridges and hydroelectric facilities were almost completely levelled. 40 kilometres of road and 19 bridges were swept away. Dozens of settlements and even whole villages were flattened. 2.2 million tonnes of debris was dumped in the disaster zone.

As of 14 September, 1,385 people are reported dead in Nepal, with 5,130 missing. The official toll in China is 43 dead and 519 missing. Several Chinese-built hydroelectric power stations in Nepal were buried, and around 900 workers were at one point unaccounted for, with dozens of them possibly still trapped in underground tunnels.

chinaworker.info express our condolences to all those who have lost their families, homes and livelihoods. However, in the face of such a massive disaster, we cannot simply “unite in grief” but need to look at why, how, and what caused this disaster.

The climate crisis – caused by capitalism’s destruction of the planet’s resources – is making such extreme events even more dangerous. The lack of democratic control by the working class and poor majority, information blackouts, and a so-called development model geared only to capitalist and geopolitical i.e. militarist interests, have further amplified the disaster.

No “negative” news

There is a stark contrast in the transparency of information between China and Nepal, despite the fact that China is far richer than Nepal with an economy 100 times bigger. Nepal has continued to publish figures on the dead, missing, and foreign travellers, whilst seeking relief supplies from foreign governments and NGOs. The Nepalese immigration authorities even utilised electronic records to reconstruct the entry records from the morning of the disaster.

On the Chinese side, however, the familiar apparatus of the CCP’s dictatorial information control was once again set in motion. In the early stages of the disaster, officials reported three deaths and several hundred missing persons; thereafter, updates to the death toll were slow to come.

Surveillance footage released by members of the public which showed the five-storey Gyirong Gate border crossing being completely demolished by the mudslide was deleted within the Great Firewall. For the Chinese dictatorship such images, which convey vulnerability and failure, are not a good fit with Beijing’s “invincible” propaganda. Beijing’s Ministry of Public Security reported that ten people had been detained accused of “spreading false information” online.

Journalists were reportedly barred from entering the disaster area on their own to interview survivors and their families. It was not until nearly two weeks after the disaster that Beijing first arranged for a small number of foreign media outlets to enter the core disaster zone.

The CCP dictatorship routinely bans “negative” news reports, operates in near total secrecy, and downplays numbers of fatalities. It did this on a massive scale during the COVID-19 pandemic. Following the sudden end of China’s ‘zero-COVID’ policy in late 2022, hospitals and crematoria were overwhelmed, yet the authorities temporarily ceased publishing figures on infections and deaths; to this day, the number of lives lost remains a mystery. Such is the logic of authoritarian rule. For the dictatorship, information is first and foremost a tool for maintaining the regime’s image and ‘social stability’, a euphemism for regime control.

How to report on the Himalayan catastrophe is an especially sensitive problem given China’s intensified repressive controls and national oppression in Tibet. In July, Beijing adopted its new ‘ethnic unity law’, which further cements the CCP’s Han chauvinist doctrine. Under this law, promoting minority languages or reporting human rights abuses are further criminalized.

Climate destruction

The Himalayan catastrophe is the latest evidence of a rapidly worsening climate crisis. Coastal provinces of China have been battered by four severe typhoons so far this year. Over 130 people were killed during “historically rare” flooding in Guangxi province. Europe has suffered from months of drought and record-breaking heat in 2026. As ISA’s Arne Johansson explains in his report, ‘Extreme Weather Disasters – The Planet is Fighting Back’, the heatwave will wipe out the entire 1% GDP growth projected in the EU this year.

The Himalayas and surrounding region are sometimes called the “Third Pole” because they contain the biggest volume of glacial ice and snow outside of the north and south poles. Likewise it is among the regions most impacted by climate change, with temperatures warming at twice the global average. China is the world’s biggest source of climate destruction, accounting for one-third of global greenhouse emissions.

This is accelerating the retreat of glaciers on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and in the Himalayas. Since 1980, there has been a marked increase in glacial lake outburst floods in the region, with the China-Nepal border being one of the areas where the risk has risen most significantly over the past decade. A 2023 paper by the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences states that potential glacial lake outbursts now threaten more than 55,000 buildings, 105 hydropower projects, and thousands of kilometres of roads and bridges.

This is by no means the first time that Gyirong has been the subject of warnings. In 2025, floods along the China-Nepal border swept away the Friendship Bridge and left many people missing. Just one year later, an even greater disaster has struck the same region.

Imperialism and geopolitical competition

Meanwhile, the capitalist CCP regime continues to regard the geologically fragile Himalayan region, an area of intense tectonic activity, as a frontline for infrastructure expansion and geopolitical competition. Here, Chinese imperialism vies for regional hegemony and control with aspiring Indian imperialism. The two neighbours engaged in a deadly border conflict in 2020 at Galwan, some 1,000 kilometres to the west of the current disaster zone. Nepal is landlocked between India and China-controlled Tibet.

Since Nepal’s then Maoist-led government in 2017 signed up for China’s imperialist ‘Belt and Road Initiative’, Chinese loans and construction in Nepal have also skyrocketed. Projects include the China-Nepal Highway and the planned China-Nepal railway.

Studies have identified hundreds of potential landslides, some of which directly threaten the highway and planned railway. Road excavation, tunnelling, hydropower and other engineering activities further increases environmental pressures in the region.

This grandiose infrastructure roll out is capitalist and imperialist in nature. It is not undertaken to improve the conditions of the local population or Nepal’s economy, but primarily to further Beijing’s drive for both “clean energy” resources and military-strategic control (to maintain its hold on Tibet). The construction frenzy may have been an additional aggravating factor behind the August disaster, magnifying the impact of climate change. The reengineering and narrowing of natural river valleys and floodplains, using millions of tonnes of concrete, could act as an accelerator and amplifier of the destructive power of floods.

China now accounts for over half of Nepal’s foreign investment. It has funded and built 12 hydropower and dam projects in Nepal – every single one of which was severely damaged or swamped during the August mudslide, according to the BBC.

Democratic working class control

Especially at a time when climate change is rapidly increasing the risks in the volatile Himalayan region, all construction projects must undergo open and democratically-controlled environmental and geological assessments. This demands a system of democratic working class control over the economic and political system, with real independent workers’ organisations and trade unions, a free working class controlled media and full equality and democratic rights for all ethnic groups. This is what real socialism means. These necessary changes are impossible within the cage of tyrannical capitalist rule under the CCP.

There is a need for full transparency regarding the number of deaths, missing persons and border crossing data in the disaster-stricken areas, an end to the media blackout, and unrestricted access for disaster victims, their families, and reporters.

All hydropower, railway, road and mining projects in Tibet and the Himalayan region must undergo geological and environmental safety assessments with veto power in the hands of the working class and local poor. Independent workers’ unions must be legalised and provided full access. High-risk areas require the establishment of transnational glacier monitoring, early warning and evacuation systems, all under democratic public ownership and control instead of prioritising ‘prestige projects’ and military expansion.

The August catastrophe is a sharp warning. In defiance of the scientific evidence and previous promises to reduce emissions and limit temperature increases, capitalists and politicians globally are now prioritising militarism, oil and coal. The struggle against climate disasters is therefore linked to the struggle against the CCP capitalist dictatorship and the global capitalist system.

title: Nepali film Elephants in the Fog selected as Nepal’s entry for 2027 Oscars - IndulgExpress
description: Nepali film Elephants in the Fog selected as Nepal’s entry for 2027 Oscars  IndulgExpress
publisher.title: IndulgExpress
full_article:
Nepali film Elephants in the Fog has reportedly made it to the list for the 99th Academy Awards. It is set to compete in the Best International Feature Film category and will represent Nepal in the 2027 Oscars. Directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, the film won the jury prize at the 79th Cannes Film Festival this year and now it is heading for an even bigger glory.

After Cannes glory, Elephants in the Fog heads to the 2027 Oscars for Nepal

Nepal’s International Feature Film Selection Committee had received two films for the Oscars nomination. Alongside Elephants in the Fog , another film Gauthali , directed by Dr. Kapil Rijal, was sent for the nomination. Following a thorough examination and evaluation based on the film’s technical and cinematic aspect, the committee decided to go ahead with the Elephants in the Fog and send it for the consideration of nomination from Nepal.

In a statement, Abinash expressing his excitement for the film’s nomination, said, “To represent Nepal on this stage is a quiet, humbling honour. This story was never mine to own, it belongs to those who carry their lives through the fog, unseen and unheard. Today, their existence step into the light, impossible to erase. That is the only victory that truly matters”.

title: New footage shows devastation of Nepal flood with over 5,000 still missing - Discover SWNS
description: New footage shows devastation of Nepal flood with over 5,000 still missing  Discover SWNS
publisher.title: Discover SWNS
full_article:
Footage from Nepal shows the devastation caused by the deadly landslide and flood that occurred last month – as more than 5,000 people remain missing.

The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).

The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.

Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.

The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

In the most recent statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Nepal on September 11, it was reported that: “13,676 people have been rescued so far, including more than 320 foreign nationals; approximately 5,130 people remain missing, including around 600 foreign nationals from approximately 35 countries; and 1,385 bodies have been recovered from the flood-affected areas.

“These figures remain subject to continuous updating as search, recovery and verification operations continue.”

In the footage, survivors can be seen salvaging whatever they can from the debris, while others stand silently at the places where their homes once stood.

Others are beginning the long process of clearing mud and debris from houses that were destroyed.

Reports say that families are still searching for missing relatives and continue to visit hospitals in Kathmandu, where they look through photographs and lists of missing people displayed on hospital walls.

People are pullied above flood water at Nuwakot, Nepal, September 14 2026.(Pixs via xStringers / SWNS)

The Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) has prepared a report on the extent of the damage caused by the disaster.

The assessment provides an initial picture of the extensive damage and needs arising from the disaster, covering the social, productive and infrastructure sectors as well as cross-cutting areas.

According to the assessment, the total damage caused by the disaster is estimated at approximately $1.8 billion (£1.3 billion), while the estimated loss is approximately $883 million.

The total estimated requirement for reconstruction is approximately $4.78 billion (£3.5 billion).

Of this, approximately $57.67 million (£42.7 million) is estimated to be required for short-term reconstruction and recovery over the next six months, while approximately $4.71 billion (£3.49 billion) is required for longer-term reconstruction.

Men shovel mud from a building in the aftermath of a flood at Nuwakot, Nepal, September 14 2026. (Pixs via xStringers / SWNS)

title: Fake image of Nepal house goes viral - Full Fact

A Facebook post from an account with more than a million followers claims to show a house in Nepal that remained standing during the recent floods. The post has thousands of likes, comments and shares.

A very similar house did survive the floods, but the image in this post was made with AI—even though a caption on it says “This home in Nuwakot, Nepal survived a flood that swept the valley away”.

When Full Fact put the image through OpenAI’s detector, it told us that it was generated with OpenAI tools.

We also gave the image to Professor Siwei Lyu, an expert in digital forensics at the University at Buffalo, and his team. He told us: “The circulating image is AI-generated. It is a synthetic re-rendering, not an authentic photograph.”

title: Climate change likely worsened conditions behind Nepal’s deadly mountain collapse - theclimatewatch.com
description: Climate change likely worsened conditions behind Nepal’s deadly mountain collapse  theclimatewatch.com
publisher.title: theclimatewatch.com
full_article:
Scientists say warming has destabilised Himalayan glaciers and frozen ground, while the disaster exposed the limits of Nepal’s existing adaptation and early warning measures.

Climate change contributed to the thinning of glaciers and thawing of frozen ground in the Himalayas, which likely played a role in the deadly rock and ice collapse in Nepal last month, according to a new scientific analysis.

The study was carried out by an international team of glaciologists and climate scientists.

More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a large section of rock and glacier collapsed from Langtang Lirung mountain on August 26. The collapse triggered a huge flow of water, ice and debris that swept through communities downstream.

Scientists said the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event. Instead, it was the result of several geological and climate-related factors coming together.

“Climate warming, caused by humans burning fossil fuels, is melting ice and snow in the Himalayas, reducing glacier coverage and thawing permafrost,” said Professor Bethan Davies, Professor of Glaciology at Newcastle University.

“This is making mountain slopes less stable and increasing the risk of disasters like this one. Urgent action is needed to reduce emissions and prevent faster melting and greater risks in the future,” she said.

According to the study, decades of warming have pushed the freezing line-the level above which temperatures remain below zero degrees Celsius-upward by about 100 metres every decade.

As a result, glaciers are retreating and frozen ground and ice inside cracks in mountain rocks are exposed to warmer temperatures for longer periods. This can weaken the slopes and make them more likely to collapse.

The researchers identified several factors that may have contributed to the collapse. Glacier thinning reduced the ice that helps stabilise mountain slopes, while increased melting may have added more water to the area.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015 may also have weakened the slope before the latest collapse. However, scientists said they cannot yet confirm how much the earthquake contributed to the 2026 disaster.

Manjeet Dhakal, Director of Climate Analytics South Asia, said the disaster was a serious warning about the growing risks faced by people living in a rapidly warming Himalaya.

“Rising temperatures are changing glaciers, snow, permafrost and the wider mountain environment, creating increasingly complex hazards,” Dhakal said.

He said the size of the disaster has tested Nepal’s ability to respond and has shown the limits of existing adaptation measures. He called for faster cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, stronger monitoring and early warning systems, better understanding of mountain risks and greater international climate finance for countries such as Nepal.

Temperatures were also unusually high just before the disaster. July and August 2026 were the warmest on record in the local area, according to the analysis. Heavy snowfall in October and November 2025 also provided additional water that later contributed to melting before the collapse.

The study found that climate change has increased July and August temperatures in the area by about 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with pre-industrial times. Climate change has increased annual temperatures in the region by about 2 degrees Celsius.

However, scientists stressed that the study does not prove that the collapse would not have happened without climate change. Instead, it shows that rising temperatures are changing the Himalayan environment and affecting several factors that can make mountain slopes unstable.

The disaster has also highlighted the limits of adaptation. Nepal has early warning systems and disaster preparedness plans, but the scale and complexity of this event were beyond the capacity of existing measures, the study said.

Professor Friederike Otto of Imperial College London said the study was different from a traditional World Weather Attribution study because it did not examine a single extreme weather event. Instead, scientists looked at a multi-stage mountain disaster involving many factors.

She said the disaster also raised an issue of climate justice, as communities in Nepal are facing the effects of a global crisis largely driven by fossil-fuel emissions.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction,” Otto said. She warned that without faster action to reduce fossil-fuel use, disasters of this scale could become more common in the future.

The researchers are calling for faster reductions in fossil-fuel emissions, stronger monitoring of glaciers and high-altitude permafrost, improved early warning systems and greater investment in understanding mountain hazards.

They also called for increased international climate finance to help vulnerable countries such as Nepal prepare for and recover from the growing risks linked to a warming Himalaya.

title: UNICEF says thousands of children require mental health support after Nepal floods - UN News
description: UNICEF says thousands of children require mental health support after Nepal floods  UN News
publisher.title: UN News
full_article:
Triggered by glacier collapse, the 26 August floods affected more than 84,000 Nepalis – including about 32,000 children – and damaged critical roads, schools, power grids and water systems across the Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading regions of northern Nepal.

Local authorities report more than 1,300 killed and more than 5,000 still missing on the Nepal side of the border, and at least 43 people killed and 519 still missing on the Tibetan side, according to official Chinese Government figures.

Tweet URL

Many children affected by the floods witnessed the loss of loved ones and the destruction of their schools while some remain displaced from their communities.

Some 541 children remain separated from their families and require protection, UNICEF reported.

“Beyond the visible destruction, these floods have left deep emotional scars on children and families,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative in Nepal. “Alongside humanitarian supplies and restoration of critical infrastructure, children need mental health and psychosocial support to help them process what happened, regain a sense of security and begin to recover.”

Why mental health support?

The flooding began at 8:37am local time – at the beginning of the school day for many children.

According to Ms. Akunga, those who witnessed distressing events are now struggling with fear, anxiety and grief, with some unable to speak about what they experienced.

Shitanshu Dhakal, a medical doctor at a hospital in Nuwakot and a mental health advocate, described the “invisible burden” of trauma on flood-affected children and the fear many still feel long after the floods.

“Children must be at the centre of the mental health response, with immediate psychological first aid and sustained support to prevent long-term consequences,” Dr. Dhakal said.

UNICEF also highlighted the importance of acting quickly. Evidence shows that early mental health intervention is critical because it can stop acute stress from becoming a lifelong chronic disorder.

Support on the ground

On the ground in Nepal, UNICEF is working with the Nepal Government and other partners to support children through family tracing, reunification and mental health services.

Eighteen children have already been reunified with their families, and 13 UNICEF-supported Child-Friendly Spaces have been established.

UNICEF is helping to arrange alternative family-based care for youngsters who have lost both parents, and monitoring teams are working to identify those at-risk and prevent exploitation.

Meanwhile, Education Cannot Wait (ECW) – the UN’s global fund for education in emergencies – announced on Tuesday a $1 million allocation to support 17,000 children across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Of those, 5,000 will receive education and protection support, while 12,000 will benefit from risk reduction interventions.

Still, with nine schools severely damaged or destroyed, ECW said Nepal’s education system will require more funding from governments, foundations and the private sector to fully rebuild from the floods.

“With climate-related emergencies disrupting children’s education with increasing frequency, we must ensure that a temporary crisis does not turn into permanent learning loss,” ECW Director of Education Maysa Jalbout said.

AIA, SEWA International Hold Bay Area Gathering For Nepal Flood Victims

India-West News Desk

OAKLAND, CA – The Association of Indo Americans (AIA), along with community partners and representatives from SEWA International – East Bay, held a remembrance and support gathering September 9 for victims of the devastating floods in Nepal.

Community members, volunteers and supporters came together to remember those who lost their lives and express solidarity with families and communities affected by the floods. The gathering included a minute of silence, followed by prayers and condolences for the victims and their families.

Representatives from Sewa shared updates on the organization’s relief efforts, including its fundraising campaign and assistance to communities affected by the floods. They also spoke about the immediate needs of families impacted by the disaster and the role of continued community support.

AIA said it is supporting Sewa International’s relief efforts and urged community members, partner organizations and others in the AIA community to contribute to the campaign.

“In times of tragedy, our strength comes from standing together. Today, we came together not only to remember the lives lost, but also to support the families and communities facing unimaginable hardship. We encourage everyone in our community to extend their support and help SEWA International in its relief efforts,” AIA said.

AIA and SEWA are encouraging individuals, families, businesses and community organizations to support the relief campaign for those affected by the Nepal floods.

title: Nepal Floods Left 268 Classrooms in Ruins. A New Scholarship Bank Aims to Rebuild What's Lost - Smiley Movement
description: Nepal Floods Left 268 Classrooms in Ruins. A New Scholarship Bank Aims to Rebuild What's Lost  Smiley Movement
publisher.title: Smiley Movement
full_article:
For two weeks now, Shanti Tamang has been turning bare displacement centres into something children can recognise: a place with drawing paper, playtime, and an adult trained to notice when a child needs more than a meal and a blanket. Her organisation, the Shanti Foundation , moved fast — child-friendly spaces went up in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot settlements within days of the flood, built for kids who lost their homes, and in some cases, their parents.

The scale of what they're up against is staggering. The 26 August flash flood tore through 32 schools, destroying 268 classrooms and disrupting learning for 9,400 students.

For families already sleeping in tents or borrowed rooms, the loss of school on top of home — and, for some, on top of a parent — has been a second collapse layered on the first.

Nepal's education ministry is now moving to catch these children before the gap widens. A new central fund, dubbed the "Scholarship Bank" , announced under the Secured Future Scholarship Scheme, promises free schooling through Grade 12 for every child displaced or orphaned by the floods, with those who lost a parent or guardian first in line.

The private sector has already answered the call: a consortium of private-school operators pledged Rs1 billion — roughly $6.62 million — enough to cover 1,000 students, through a mix of full residential scholarships and partial aid scaled to what each family can bear.

But money and enrollment forms only solve half the problem. Aid organisations on the ground say the emotional toll is just as urgent children separated from caregivers, or living in unstructured temporary settlements, face real risks of disease and exploitation that a supervised, structured space helps hold at bay.

Tamang's foundation is one of several stepping into that gap while the slower machinery of formal reunification and school enrollment grinds into motion.

The scholarship scheme's fine print — who qualifies, how fast aid reaches them — is still being worked out. And that's the crux of it: the next few weeks will decide how many of those 9,400 students walk back into a classroom before the school year simply moves on without them.

What it will take: funding for the Scholarship Bank that outlasts this first wave of private pledges, and continued support for the quieter, daily work like Tamang's that keeps children steady while everything else around them is still being rebuilt.

Charity check-in

At Smiley Movement, we like to elevate the work of charities across the world. Here are three charities whose causes align with the themes in this article.

Shanti Foundation. This Nepal-based nonprofit sets up child-friendly spaces within displacement settlements, giving children who've lost homes and parents a safe, structured place to be cared for by trained staff. Find out more .

Save the Children. This international children's charity has run programmes in Nepal since 1976 and mobilised rapidly after the August 2026 floods, working across shelter, family tracing and reunification, psychosocial support, and access to education. Find out more here.

UNICEF. This UN agency has scaled up its emergency response across the flood-hit districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, tracing and reunifying unaccompanied children, dispatching education supplies, and establishing temporary learning spaces for the tens of thousands of school-age children whose education was disrupted. Support them here.

title: Marie Colvin Center Enables Global Connections Amid Deadly Floods in Nepal - SBU News
description: Marie Colvin Center Enables Global Connections Amid Deadly Floods in Nepal  SBU News
publisher.title: SBU News
full_article:
Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel

When disaster struck Nepal, Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel ‘24 connected with a former visiting scholar at the Marie Colvin Center for International Reporting to obtain eyewitness testimony of the flooding for O Globo, one of Brazil’s leading newspapers.

On August 26, a glacial collapse near the Nepal-China border triggered flash floods, mudslides and debris flow. The impact of the collapse was equivalent to an M5.2 earthquake. More than 1,300 people were killed in Nepal and Tibet, with approximately 5,000 people missing.

Cruvinel traveled to Nepal as a foreign reporter in the Colvin Center’s 2024 Journalism Without Walls program . The visit was coordinated by Shraddha Verma, a Colvin international scholar in Fall 2023 .

Cruvinel is based in Rio de Janeiro for a training program at O Globo . Working as a journalist, he reached out to Verma, who worked until recently as an expert in child trafficking issues and an advocate for young women’s rights in Nepal.

Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel’s story in O Globo .

“Shraddha was able to help me, and a few hours later I was talking to two people impacted by the floods. My report ended up going in the print paper, as well as being posted online,” said Cruvinel.

While a journalism student at Stony Brook, Cruvinel won a Hearst Journalism Award in feature writing and was managing editor of The Stony Brook Press . After graduating from the School of Communication and Journalism, Cruvinel completed a master’s degree in publishing at New York University before returning to his native Brazil.

“I am proud of the global connections the Colvin Center has been able to foster,” said Sarah Baxter, director of the Colvin Center. “Rafael is an outstanding trilingual journalist who is making the most of the skills and contacts he acquired through Stony Brook.”

The Center’s Journalism Without Walls program has granted foreign reporting opportunities for students in Berlin , Sweden , Moldova , Kenya and Korea . Next summer’s destination will be Argentina.

Colvin international scholars have been hosted from Cambodia, Slovakia , Ukraine , Moldova , Indonesia and the West Bank through the IREX Community Solutions program.

— Melanie Formosa

How 2015 Earthquake Lessons Guide Response to Nepal's Recent "Himalayan Tsunami"

By Noah Smith

After the August 26th floods in Nepal, reports reaching Gordon Willcock in Kathmandu described families who had lost more than their homes. Willcock, Direct Relief's Asia Pacific regional director, said that many farmers had lost what they knew as their land, after river valleys were buried in mud and silt.

Willcock, who was also on the ground after the devastating 2015 earthquakes in Nepal, which killed more than 8,000 people, described some key differences between the two disasters. With the August floods, given the scale of transformation, some communities might have to relocate altogether.

"In an earthquake, buildings in a localized area are destroyed, but then you can rebuild. In this disaster, it's not like you can excavate and rebuild your house. It's done," Willcock said of the recent floods.

Both the remoteness of the impacted areas and geomorphic change introduced new challenges compared to the capital city-based earthquakes. Revealingly, locals felt the term "flood" failed to cover the totality of what occurred.

Residents called it a "Himalayan tsunami," Willcock said of the flooding and debris flow that killed more than 1,400 people. More than 5,300 remain missing.

In 2015, following an earthquake registering at least 7.8-magnitude in strength, Willcock had flown from his home in Melbourne alongside journalists and search-and-rescue teams, arriving at a chaotic Kathmandu airport.

Since Direct Relief’s network in-country at the time was sparse, much of his early work in the capital involved visiting hospitals, meeting as many relevant contacts as possible, and determining what they needed.

Many of those meetings resulted in partnerships that have spanned more than a decade. Dhulikhel Hospital was one of several groups involved in the 2015 earthquake response that deployed in the hours after the August 2026 floods with pre-positioned aid from Direct Relief.

Comparing Disaster Impacts: 2015 Earthquake vs. Recent Nepal Floods

As part of the ongoing flood response, Willcock wasn't able to go to the most devastated areas due to infrastructure damage, but benefited from the relationships he had helped originate years prior. From Kathmandu, he could gather information from organizations responding in the affected valleys and help coordinate support.

Comparing the two natural disasters, Willcock said that medical needs differed.

He recalled sustained demand for trauma care after the 2015 earthquake, including treatment for crush injuries. After the August 2026 floods’ initial emergency, displacement and interrupted access to chronic disease medications quickly became central concerns, he said.

Flood-destroyed roads in rural areas compounded nearly every need, including access to food, shelter, medicine and electricity. Damaged roads also blocked patients' access to functioning medical facilities; Dhulikhel Hospital sent doctors and surgeons by helicopter to support other hospitals and displaced people.

In a Sept. 11 update, Direct Relief reported that a Mountain Heart Nepal mission to Kalika Rural Municipality in Rasuwa district took nearly 12 hours, about twice the usual journey. The team delivered medical supplies and provided treatment and counseling.

Supplies positioned before the disaster helped local teams begin responding immediately. Dhulikhel Hospital deployed with Direct Relief emergency medical backpacks already on hand. Another 14 tons of medical aid arrived in Kathmandu on Sept. 6, including antibiotics, IV fluids and medications for chronic conditions.

Those efforts also address health risks beyond initial injuries: unsafe water, disrupted maternal care and the difficulty of maintaining treatment while displaced.

Local Partnerships Drive Rapid Emergency Medical Response

For Willcock, strong, lasting partnerships provide what he called "the best disaster preparedness we have."

Relationships established during the earthquake response, and maintained through subsequent support, allowed Direct Relief to identify needs more quickly and support organizations already reaching affected communities.

He described this response as more Nepal-led, with local charities, health workers and government agencies mobilizing rapidly. International organizations, he said, should strengthen that work and coordinate with existing authorities.

The work ahead, Willcock cautioned, would stretch far beyond the emergency. Recent mudflows and wildfires, even in wealthy California communities such as Montecito and Malibu, have taken years, he noted.

As was the case after 2015, Willcock said Direct Relief will continue to respond to requested needs from local partners, who are now helping communities through another disaster.

"One main learning as an organization is the importance of having strong long-term partnerships, which become the best disaster preparedness we have. They're the foundation from which we respond," he said.

title: Building a Palliative Care Network in Nepal: A New Model from Koshi Province - Oncodaily
description: Building a Palliative Care Network in Nepal: A New Model from Koshi Province  Oncodaily
publisher.title: Oncodaily
full_article:
In resource-constrained healthcare systems, the intersection of acute oncology care, chronic symptom burden, and advanced disease management presents a formidable challenge. Tertiary center beds and intensive care units are routinely overwhelmed by complex chronic and terminal patients whose care can be effectively optimized outside tertiary settings, yet who lack access to structured palliative support in their communities.

To bridge this critical gap, a transformative pilot workshop was organized by the Nepal Hospice Care Center (NHCC) in collaboration with B.P. Koirala Institute of Health Sciences (BPKIHS),supported by Two Worlds Cancer Collaboration (TWCC), Canada, bringing together frontline doctors and nurses from all 14 districts of Koshi Province.

The Hub-and-Spoke Ecosystem, with BPKIHS serving as the central hub, is developing a decentralized, four-pillar framework designed to expand palliative care expertise across the province:

Home-Based Hospice and Palliative Care: Dedicated regional clinical teams providing holistic symptom management and compassionate support directly in community settings. Intensive Workforce Capacity Building: Evidence-based training in symptom control, pain management, opioid protocols, and compassionate communication. Telemedicine & Referral Networks: A permanent digital cord connecting district health workers with tertiary specialists for real-time case consultations. Mobile Outreach & Field Mentorship: Direct on-site mentorship across the 14 districts to supervise community nurses and ensure quality delivery.

Optimizing Bed Triage and Human Dignity Beyond compassionate patient support, the model serves as an indispensable tool for healthcare resource optimization. By empowering trained physicians and community nurses to manage complex symptom trajectories and advanced illness locally, the program aims to reduce potentially avoidable hospital and ICU admissions and ease pressure on inpatient services.

A nation-wide sustainable framework developed by Dr. Soniya Dulal under the expert mentorship of Prof. Dr. Bishnu Dutta Paudel and supported by global expertise from the Two Worlds Cancer Collaboration (TWCC), the initiative is powered by strong multi-sectoral synergy between the Koshi Provincial Government and the Dharan Sub-Metropolitan City.

This project demonstrates that decentralized palliative care is not merely an ethical imperative—it is an operational necessity. As Koshi Province establishes this regional network, it lays the cornerstone for a scalable, sustainable national model across Nepal.

Kathmandu, Sept 15: Nepal has established its diplomatic ties today with the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). With this, the number of countries with which Nepal has established diplomatic relations has reached 185.

Lok Bahadur Thapa, the Permanent Representative of Nepal to the United Nations, and Jeem S. Lippwe, the Permanent Representative of the Federated States of Micronesia to the United Nations, signed a joint statement to this effect, according to the Permanent Mission of Nepal to the UN.

On the occasion, the two representatives exchanged views on cooperating with each in various areas of mutual interest, including in national and international forums.

Micronesia, an island nation, in the western Pacific Ocean comprises more than 600 islands. It gained independence on November 3, 1986, and became a member of the United Nations on September 17, 1991.

The country covers a total area of 701 square kilometres and is home to an estimated population of 100,000. Both Nepal and Micronesia are members of the Group of 77(G77).(RSS)

Cross-border devastation
